#523. Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time

Now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times."

Atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A New Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times

The researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

"It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a new technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times."

That improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A New Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity

The findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening new possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

For now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

"Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the big next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics."

If successful, such experiments could offer scientists a new way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

#519. Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion

The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave, but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

#518. Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

"This idea that relativity is important in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," said Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements."

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

Atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

Some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

The sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

For lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

Heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become important, changing how the electrons behave.

One particularly important effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

"The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang said. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore."

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds

To test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

Bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

The researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

By measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

Rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks

The findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

Bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang said.

The research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

#517. 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson

For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon.

Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth. Johnson is home to NASA’s Orion and Moon Base programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health.

When the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away. Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the new Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued. The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk. Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program. Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968.  Managers in Houston devised a daring plan to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight.

In December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.”  Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration in December 1972.

Following the Moon landings, scientists at the Manned Spacecraft Center’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory conducted initial analyses of Apollo lunar samples and prepared them for researchers around the world. After the building was demolished in March 2024, the Lunar Receiving Park was dedicated to honor the laboratory’s history in 2026. Today, Johnson’s Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division continues to analyze and curate the Apollo collection at the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility.

Skylab, America’s first space station, ran into trouble during its launch in May 1973, losing its thermal shield, jamming one solar array and losing the other one.  In less than 10 days, engineers in Houston designed and built a sun shield and generated procedures to free the jammed array, followed by the first extensive in-orbit repair activities by the first Skylab crew. The three missions lasting 28, 59, and 84 days accomplished more research than planned, demonstrated the value of humans on long-duration missions, and provided operators in mission control with round-the-clock experience monitoring long duration human spaceflights.

In July 1975, after several joint training sessions in Houston and Moscow, American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts met in space for the first time during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. Approved as a project in 1972, five approach and landing tests of the space shuttle using orbiter Enterprise paved the way for the first orbital mission of Columbia in 1981.

Engineers in Houston began designs for a reuseable space plane in the late 1960s, with the space shuttle receiving formal approval in 1972. During the 1970s, Johnson Space Center put in place the training and simulation facilities that astronauts used for the life of the program. Upgrades to mission control enabled the use of the latest technologies to support ever more complex space shuttle missions. The April 1981 launch of space shuttle Columbia inaugurated a new era of reusable spacecraft. The program’s 135 missions flew 355 individuals from 16 nations. Missions included satellite deployments and retrievals, dedicated Department of Defense flights, a variety of science missions including deployment of planetary spacecraft, ferrying crews and cargo to two different space stations, and doing the heavy lifting in the assembly of the orbiting laboratory. The program recovered from the tragic losses of the Challenger and Columbia crews with renewed emphasis on crew safety. The final space shuttle mission, STS-135, closed out the 30-year program in July 2011.

An Earth orbiting space station, first approved by President Ronald Reagan in 1984, underwent many modifications before taking on its current form as the International Space Station in 1993. Overall management of the program resides at Johnson. The first element launch took place in November 1998, followed one month later by the first U.S. element, the Node 1 Unity module. The first expedition crew took up residence on Nov. 2, 2000, and for more than 26 years, rotating crews of astronauts and cosmonauts have lived and worked aboard the orbiting laboratory, establishing a permanent human presence in low Earth orbit.

To date, 298 individuals from 26 countries have visited the space station, conducting more than 4,000 science experiments and educational activities to enable exploration missions and improve life on Earth.

Life aboard the space station depends on a global team on the ground. Crews conduct research and maintain equipment in microgravity, while Johnson teams at the Mission Control Center coordinate the agency’s station operations with international partners. Johnson’s Space Vehicle Mockup Facility supports training for NASA astronauts and international crews on station systems, science operations, and emergency procedures. At the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory, crews rehearse spacewalks around full-scale station mockups in one of the world’s largest indoor pools. Johnson’s Human Research Program also supports health investigations aboard the station, helping researchers understand how spaceflight affects the body so crews can thrive on future deep space missions.

What began as a framework of modules has evolved into a springboard for international cooperation, advanced scientific research and technology demonstrations, the development of a low Earth orbit economy, and NASA’s next giant leaps in exploration. The space station continues to be a proving ground for NASA’s Artemis program and human exploration of Mars.

The Artemis II mission marked the first crewed flight of NASA’s Orion spacecraft. The four-person crew launched April 1, on a nearly 10-day trip around the Moon. At its farthest point, Orion traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had traveled before. The mission demonstrated Orion’s capabilities with astronauts aboard and tested crew operations in deep space, setting the stage for future lunar missions.

Building on Artemis II, NASA’s Artemis III mission will test integrated operations in low Earth orbit between Orion and test versions of one or both commercial human landing systems under development by SpaceX and Blue Origin. Astronauts will demonstrate the rendezvous and docking capabilities needed to transfer crews between spacecraft for the lunar landing planned for Artemis IV.

NASA’s Moon Base Program is planning a phased effort to support a sustained human presence near the Moon’s South Pole region. The first phase will focus on robotic exploration, technology demonstrations, and preparations for future surface operations. Later phases will add infrastructure to support astronauts living and working on the Moon. Lunar terrain vehicles will help crews explore farther, transport equipment, and conduct science.

At Johnson, teams are drawing on decades of experience in astronaut training, mission control, spacecraft development, and human health to prepare for these missions. From training crews for lunar operations to developing the systems that will support them, Johnson is building on 65 years of human spaceflight experience for humanity’s return to the lunar surface through the Artemis and Moon Base Programs.

These strange geological features may offer clues to the Red Planet's watery past.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.

While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.

In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.

NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency.

Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day, or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis.

Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape.

Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA.

Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scientists determine how the rocks formed and whether they preserve potential signs of past microbial activity.

Back at Mount Sharp, Curiosity has also spotted another geological curiosity: the return of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns across the Martian bedrock.

The rover's latest images, captured on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073), show small, regularly shaped polygons outlined by raised ridges, resembling patterns the rover encountered earlier in its climb up the layered mountain, whose rocky slopes preserve a record of Mars' changing climate and ancient watery environments. Scientists say these formations could have developed through several processes, including mineral shrinkage as water evaporated, temperature changes or the expansion and compaction of buried sediments, according to a statement from NASA.

By studying the composition of the rocks and the material cementing the raised ridges around the polygons, researchers hope to determine which processes shaped the terrain.

Together, these discoveries highlight how much Mars' seemingly barren landscape can reveal about its past. As Curiosity continues climbing Mount Sharp and Perseverance investigates ancient terrain beyond Jezero Crater, both rovers are helping piece together the planet's unique features and complex geological history.

#515. A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

The biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

New research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."

Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."

The researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths

Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

By studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

#513. Laser Focus at the Top of the World

A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.

More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a new, more precise method for tracking satellites.

Since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory—laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide.

In 2026, the next generation of SLR, developed by NASA scientists and tested at Goddard, began to come online. On October 12, a faster, even more precise SLR system officially debuted at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, operated by the Norwegian Mapping Authority, a NASA partner. The observatory’s remote location in the Arctic archipelago is shown in this image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 in July 2026. It is the first NASA next-generation SLR system in operation and the northernmost SLR facility on Earth.

While the systems developed decades ago have been “workhorses” of the global laser tracking network, their age and the growing number of satellites have necessitated updates, said Stephen Merkowitz, project manager for NASA’s Space Geodesy Project. “We wanted newer systems that could track more objects, and track them more accurately and precisely,” he said.

Years of development, testing, and careful calibration produced the Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system now running at Ny-Ålesund. Among its features are lasers that can fire pulses thousands of times per second, up from tens of times per second, and sensors that can detect single photons, meaning that less light needs to be reflected back from a satellite.

Along with determining the orbits of satellites, SLR is critical for establishing the terrestrial reference frame, the foundation of modern coordinate systems and a common standard that allows measurements to be compared with one another. “If you want to know where your satellite observation is on a map, you need to have it in the proper reference frame,” Merkowitz said. In addition, tracking Earth’s center of mass, measuring changes in sea level and ice mass, studying the motion of tectonic plates, and maintaining global navigation satellite systems such as GPS, all rely on an accurate reference frame.

The far-north location of the Ny-Ålesund facility improves the distribution of SLR stations across the planet, making the whole network more robust. The location also allows the system to gather more data about polar-orbiting satellites, which include ICESat-2, GRACE-FO, and other Earth observation satellites. “From the station at Goddard [in Greenbelt, Maryland], we’ll catch the polar-orbiting satellites maybe two or three times a day,” Merkowitz said. “But from Ny-Ålesund, you’ll see them almost every orbit.”

Certain satellite missions may especially benefit from the Arctic location, he added. Take ICESat-2, designed to make precise observations of ice surface heights. Having a station tracking the satellite from an icy polar region could lead to more accurate measurements there. “When it’s over the ice, we want the calibration to be as good as possible,” Merkowitz said.

Innovations and lessons learned from the Svalbard installation will carry over to future ones, Merkowitz said. In particular, the Ny-Ålesund facility drove improvements in automation because the site is located next to a bird sanctuary. Access restrictions require the station to be remotely operated at certain times, such as during the summer breeding season for migratory birds. These capabilities can be refined and applied at other stations. NASA is currently building two more next-generation SLR systems to replace legacy instruments at Goddard and the McDonald Geodetic Observatory in Texas.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. NASA photo by Julie Horvath (KBR). Story by Lindsey Doermann.

Before New Shepard all boosters were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever.

After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground. This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history.

The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.

Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms.

But in the end, Blue Origin did it first.

Blue Origin's New Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket.

Since that first landing, Blue Origin has launched 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company announced a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects.

But Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the company's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown.

Blue Origin has since reflown a New Glenn booster, and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance.

#510. DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.

Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

The research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides new insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.

Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists

One of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An important difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.

This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.

Why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.

To explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.

DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage

The results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an important advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.

"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," said Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule."

This finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.

The discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an important role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.

New Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection

Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.

The team established a new set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.

"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," said Khosh Abady.

These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.

Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?

With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team plan to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.

A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.

"We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins."

By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.

How realistic are the zero-g sports we see in sci-fi? We talk to Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, to find out.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics. The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation, the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut.

Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game. There was even Space Jam's alien basketball game for the fate of the planet, though the gravity-defying antics there come from cartoon shenanigans rather than a zero-g playing field.

As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play.

We rarely think about it in an Earth context, but every sport is heavily influenced by gravity. It defines how balls arc, how quickly players can move, and even how we orient ourselves in play spaces. Remove the gravity, and all of those assumptions and mechanics evaporate as well.

"First of all, in zero g, Isaac Newton will win every time," Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, told Space. Les is a physicist with over 35 years of experience working at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, as well as a science fiction author.

"'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction,'" quotes Johnson. "This is very difficult to simulate in real life due to gravity; special effects often try to compensate. With today’s AI and green screens, it can actually look good on screen."

In a microgravity scenario, the concept of up and down is no longer relevant. Suddenly, the playing field expands from a single, fixed plane to a fully three-dimensional space that includes height.

Momentum is also a completely different beast. Instead of being able to quickly stop and pivot the way you can during terrestrial sports, once you start moving in microgravity, you keep going until something stops you. It takes the trickiness of moving on ice in sports like hockey and increases it by several orders of magnitude.

Of course, the havoc wouldn't stop with maneuvering yourself. Any ball or other object would also be subject to this altered set of physics.

As Johnson points out, "Aside from maneuvering the body and not tumbling or going in the wrong direction, the most difficult part would probably be throwing or hitting a ball in zero g. There would be no arc, just a straight-line throw. That would take getting used to doing, given that we’ve spent our entire lives calculating how high and fast to throw a ball in 1G so it gets to the person we intend."

Science fiction interpretations have often leaned into these differences; in many cases, low-g sports look more like three-dimensional chess than the highly physical contests we're used to here on Earth.

Ironically, many of the best examples of space-based sports are the most grounded, where real-world physics are fully accounted for.

2013's "Ender's Game" gives us one of the best examples of a zero-g arena in space. Dubbed the "Battle Room," it's a giant hollow cube filled with obstacles. Teams enter through gates at opposite ends and participate in laser tag-style drills while having to grapple with three-dimensional space, while also finding ways to propel and protect themselves.

"The Battle Room sequence does a great job of thinking about straight‑line, constant‑velocity motion," Johnson said. "No 'reaction' to slow you down or change your direction. Characters push off walls or each other, then drift until they hit something or fire their suit's thrusters."

Johnson said Ender's Game also did an admirable job of showcasing how alternate physics require another layer of planning when moving through space.

"They went to great lengths to show that there was no preferred 'up' or 'down'. Again, very accurate and realistic thinking. Floating obstacles in the battle space created realistic constraints: if you don't think about where you'll rebound, you can pin yourself behind an obstacle or drift out of the fight."

Recognizing how important play can be (and, perhaps, acknowledging ways to combat the lingering specter of space madness), real-world space agencies have begun brainstorming what recreation in low gravity might look like. Some proposed ideas include 3D ball games not wholly dissimilar from the Battle Room, where players enter a cube or spherical arena and push off walls/pass a ball in any direction, scoring by hitting targets.

Elastic tethers are another experimental concept being bandied around, where players are connected to flexible tethers to improve movement control and cut down on collisions. The Space Games Federation has also floated the idea of a version of space basketball, where the goal is guiding a magnetic ball through hoops, as well as some version of space dodgeball.

Of course, these proposals are nothing more than thought exercises at the moment. We're a long way out from vast human populations living in zero-g environments for extended periods of time, and even further still from building spaceships capable of housing a sports hall.

NASA astronauts have experimented with trying to play various terrestrial sports in space, usually aboard the International Space Station. We've seen them playing soccer, lacrosse, and hockey with varying degrees of success.

These fun experiments mainly serve to prove what we've already suspected: that terrestrial sports can't be directly translated into a zero-g environment. We'll need new rules, arenas, and whole new games if we're going to make any headway with competitive sports in space.

Sci-fi has a pretty good track record for simulating open 3D environments in microgravity. The genre also tends to do fairly well in depicting the methodical pace of moving through space and how that would affect competition (and combat).

Games like "Echo Arena" even use technology to help simulate these factors. Echo Arena is a VR game where you boost around a zero-g arena, punching opponents and trying to toss a disc into a goal.

The game's innovative movement system allows players to grab almost any surface, either moving themselves along it or pushing off to float in a given direction. Players are also given wrist-mounted thrusters to let them course-correct a little, offering a respite from the unforgiving laws of motion.

Dead Space also has a section that functions similarly but with conventional game controls, though the only sport there is "don't get eaten by necromorphs."

With that said, there are areas where sci-fi portrayals of zero-G games fall down. Energy levels and fatigue is a big one: constant maneuvering with your arms is exhausting, which is why real astronauts rely heavily on handholds. In a similar vein, there's the issue of infinite momentum, specifically as it applies to rotation.

Johnson specifically quibbles with scenes in the Ender's Game Battle Room and "how quickly the participants can rotate their bodies or part of their bodies without going into an uncontrollable spin." He points to incidents where real-life astronauts have demonstrated how challenging this phenomenon would actually be. "I’ve watched many videos of astronauts on the ISS twist and then bounce off the wall or something. They have all looked very clumsy when they do this."

The other kind of space constraints are also often hand-waved. Even the largest existing spacecraft pale in comparison to the size of stadiums or arenas on Earth. Our early attempts at space-based sports will likely have to be centered in much smaller playing areas.

Safety issues are frequently downplayed as well; colliding with metal surfaces at high speeds in enclosed environments risks serious bodily harm to players as well as potential damage to suits/gear.

With that said, newer sci-fi portrayals are getting closer to reality by emphasizing slower, more deliberate movement and placing the focus on strategic thinking rather than athletic prowess.

In the meantime, astronauts might have to stick to video games to scratch their competitive itches.

Alan Bradley is an experienced tech and culture writer with more than 20 years covering gaming, tech, and hardware. His work has appeared in Rolling Stone, U.S. News & World Report, PCMag, TechRadar, GamesRadar+, CNET, Live Science, Variety, and many other outlets.

#506. A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.

The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve important biological functions.

In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.

Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation

One of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting important cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.

To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.

They found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.

The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.

This research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal important new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.

"We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," said Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.

He added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject."

Gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.

Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?

The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.

By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.

"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," said Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.

He added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine."

Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.

Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island

Jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.

He arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.

The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.

Today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

#505. NASA’s Webb Shows How Supernova Dust Chronicles Star Evolution

NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets.

This high-resolution, mid-infrared observation from Webb reveals new details that are helping astronomers chronicle the structure and evolution of Cas A’s original star. The Webb data supports a scenario in which the interior of the star underwent a dramatic change, possibly just hours before its demise. These results published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Stars begin their lives as large clouds of mostly hydrogen gas and cosmic dust called molecular clouds. Eventually, gravity causes these molecular clouds to collapse, the material heats up, and protostars — infant stars — form. Under the constant pressure of gravity, hydrogen within a protostar begins to fuse into helium, which marks the point where protostars evolve into full-fledged stars like our Sun.

As hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats until helium begins to fuse into heavier elements. This process repeats as stars like Cas A’s original star evolve, with increasingly heavier elements fusing in the core (eventually stopping at iron) and lighter elements fusing in surrounding layers. This leads to multiple shells of elements that provide a record of a star’s evolutionary history. When a star goes supernova, these elements are scattered into the surrounding space, where some of them condense to form dust grains, which can clump together. By studying and mapping the composition of these individual, solar-system-sized dust clumps in Cas A, Webb found evidence of a shell merger, a process in which the layers inside a star mix before the explosion.

“Material within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,” said Tea Temim, lead author of the study and research scientist from Columbia University in New York. “So, for example, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merge together and change the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.”

For the researchers to know where to look with Webb, they also leveraged data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope. Although it couldn’t resolve the minute details of the region during its observation, Spitzer identified three specific regions to observe with Webb’s keen eye.

Two of the targets were inside Cas A’s reverse-shocked region, where an inward-moving shock wave collides with debris thrown outward by the supernova. Webb observed that the ejecta in one of the two contained mostly silica dust, while the other was dominated by carbon dust. The third target was the “Green Monster,” a structure first discovered by Webb, which was found to be rich in complex magnesium silicates. Unlike the other two regions, the Green Monster originated from material the star shed before it exploded, rather than from the supernova’s ejecta.

Building on the X-ray observations of NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the JAXA-led XRISM, Webb mapped the dust composition of Cas A across the entire remnant, providing crucial insight into the shell merger phenomenon. Together, these observations indicate that the merger was underway very shortly before the supernova explosion.

“With Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,” said Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana. “As a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. It’s telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.”

The dust map from Webb also reveals that the merger signatures are present throughout much of the supernova remnant. These efforts provide a new method for other astronomers who want to infer characteristics about an originating star’s structure by using the dust of a supernova remnant.

The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

#504. Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."
