#384. Google Workspace Promo Codes: 14% Off for November 2026

Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.

Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.

There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.

Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.

Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.

Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.

Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.

At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.

Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.

Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.

You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.

Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.

Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.

Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.

#379. Booking Holdings creates new enterprise division as AI reshapes travel planning

Booking Holdings is bringing together two of its business-to-business travel operations in a new division it hopes will be transformational, betting that a larger, coordinated partner platform can generate growth as artificial intelligence changes how travelers discover and book trips.

The new enterprise unit, dubbed Booking Partner Division, will combine Booking.com Strategic Partnerships with Rocket Travel by Agoda, and is set to begin operating in January. Agoda CEO Omri Morgenshtern will lead the unit, which aims to help businesses such as banks, airlines and online travel companies sell trips or build branded experiences for their customers.

"We realize that if we focus our efforts both on the product side, but also on the go-to-market side, then we can potentially grow faster and serve better partners," Morgenshtern told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

He said existing partners will find new and better products, which will also help grow the partner base.

The move gives Booking a single organization to coordinate technology, travel supply and commercial expertise across business relationships. The company says partners will be able to use its global supply and technology through white-label platforms, integrated applications, branded solutions and hotel-chain rate distribution.

The portfolio includes more than 4.7 million properties, 33 million accommodation listings, more than 500 airlines and more than 200 car rental providers, according to the company.

Competitor Expedia Group has seen notable growth by prioritizing its enterprise efforts, including a strategy launched in 2022 to make its technology platform available to business partners looking to add travel to their own offerings.

From 2018 to 2023, Expedia’s business-to-business revenue grew at a 16% compound annual rate, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, for the division grew at a 28% rate, the company said in 2024.

In 2025, Expedia’s B2B revenue rose 18% to $4.8 billion, and its segment adjusted EBITDA increased 22% to $1.26 billion. Those figures represented about a third of Expedia’s total revenue and more than a third of its adjusted EBITDA for the full year.

Morgenshtern declined to say how much the new division is expected to contribute to Booking Holdings' overall revenue and profit, but he said the opportunity for growth is immense, estimating the total addressable market at $2 trillion.

Online travel agencies have been pressured this year as investors scrutinize how AI will change the way customers search for and then book their travel.

Companies that offer lodging, experiences and other travel and leisure are grappling with how to stay visible if AI tools become the new starting point for planning and reservations.

Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro said on the company’s earnings call Tuesday that guests already use AI to discover and plan Disney trips, and that some are using the tools to book.

“Ultimately, we want Disney to show up in those tools,” he said, adding that Disney is exploring ways to let guests make reservations directly from them.

Booking anticipates offering partners AI capabilities that draw on the company's existing travel know-how while minimizing token costs, it said.

"I see a lot of AI demos," Morgenshtern said, drawing a distinction between a product that caters to a few customers and one that's scalable and works even when overloaded by travel emergencies. He said he's "super optimistic" about the bespoke product — a vertical agent — that Booking will offer to its partners.

At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

For the best savings, consider the 12-month plan. It has a higher upfront fee of $180, but it breaks down to $15 a month. Unlike the three-month plan, it stays at $15 after it renews (subject to potential price increases, which are very possible given the nature of subscription services). You pay more at first, but you save even more over time.

Perhaps the best feature for seniors is Mint Mobile’s customer service, staffed by live agents by phone during select hours or available 24/7 via online chat. While many companies are increasingly moving toward AI-based systems, having humans who can help guide customers through issues is refreshing.

Like seniors, Mint Mobile doesn’t offer plans or discounts for kids. Instead, parents can choose a low-cost option that fits their children’s mobile habits. If they rely mostly on Wi-Fi at home, school, or the library, they may not need a high-data plan. If they binge on streaming entertainment and are constantly on social media, Mint offers 17 GB, 23 GB, or unlimited data plans at $20, $25, or $30 per month.

As mentioned above, the different monthly terms (3, 6, and 12 months) require different upfront payments, and prices may also increase after the initial entry price. The best approach is for parents to determine their child’s needs, then browse Mint’s plans that fit their budget. It can get costly as you move up in data and monthly tiers, plus the higher upfront costs, but parents could still save money in the long run compared with a legacy carrier, and without a contract. If additional children also need a phone plan, parents should look at family plans offered by other service providers. Mint Mobile doesn’t offer a traditional family plan, but you can sign up for multiple plans and mix and match based on your needs. Again, do some price comparison to see if you would actually save money.

Something Mint Mobile doesn’t offer is a smartwatch plan. Instead of phones, a popular trend is for parents to give their kids a cellular-enabled Apple Watch. So if this is what you’re looking for, sadly, Mint Mobile won’t work for this purpose.

Mint offers home internet from its parent, T-Mobile. Like its phone plans, Mint offers Home Minternet packages in 3-, 6-, or 12-month terms, each with an upfront payment. Prices start at $40 per month for a three-month term ($120 upfront).

Right now, Mint Mobile is offering a 12-month plan for $45 per month ($540 upfront) that bundles 12 months of unlimited data—a $300 savings compared with buying both separately. Since home internet can easily cost double what Mint charges, this could be a significant cost-saver for those with modest internet needs that T-Mobile’s 5G network can handle.

#374. Lowe's posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market

Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers.

The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion.

Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat.

CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years.

"We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC.

Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers.

He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects.

"We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program."

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior.

The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates.

Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year.

Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter.

"So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said.

Ellison told CNBC the company remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far.

Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.

#371. The Manosphere Isn’t Ready for Brothercore

On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.

“The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr. pauses to explain to a group of eight similarly fit, sweaty, nearly all shirtless men who are watching the action in a circle. Monteon is a wrestler and influencer from Arizona, with pomelo-sized biceps, glossy shoulder-length hair, and more than 675,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram. He turns to his demo partner, Johnny Cole, a rangy, then 28-year-old content creator (59,000 TikTok followers) with a penchant for slutty tank tops. “And this one is called the Saturday night ride.”

Monteon and Cole continue scuffling. The match ends with Monteon straddling Cole, their faces inches apart, their torsos glistening. The scene looks like a JV wrestling match.

The other men pair up to take turns grappling. Two cameramen circle them as a drone hums overhead.

“Yes, testosterone!” one influencer yells.

“And estrogen!” Cole adds. “Both of them together, as one!”

I’m at Hey Brother House, a content incubator that hosts weeklong retreats for male social media influencers. The organization teaches men and boys “to embody healthy masculinity, fully process emotions, embrace authenticity, and show up as compassionate, empathetic community leaders,” according to its website.

Filmmaker Vince Nett captures the shirtless shenanigans of Carlos Monteon Jr.

Cole, the founder of Hey Brother, helms the project with two other house leaders. Jonathan Jacobs, an affable 37-year-old who owns a digital marketing agency in Los Angeles, is wearing a brown cap that says “Male Friendship.” Matthew Echelman, a 35-year-old Brooklyn-based filmmaker, has hired two crew members to film the whole thing for a possible future documentary. Funded by a grant of more than $180,000 from an initiative called the Young Men and Media Collective, Hey Brother House’s goal is to flood 18-to-25-year-old men’s social media feeds with content that will (hopefully) make them less terrible.

The house itself is a rented stucco McMansion next to the Green Valley Ranch Golf Club, a residential community just outside Denver. In some respects, it looks like your average fratty domicile: There’s a Nintendo Switch console in the living room, where the boys play Mario Kart; a basement decked out with fitness equipment, a sauna, air hockey, and Foosball; and a makeshift indoor putting green. But there’s also a strict house alcohol ban, remote-controlled bidets, a box of wigs, swag boxes filled with fuchsia “Redefining Masculinity” T-shirts, and a wall covered in Post-Its of “gifts” the men can give each other, including “laying down on couch or blanket in park with my head on your lap.” There’s even a room—the “Man Box”—for testimonials, where the “cast members” can speak directly to the camera about their day. It’s reminiscent of reality TV, except most everyone is aware of bell hooks’ All About Love: New Visions, and they are explicitly here to make friends.

These guys are all in Denver because, as Cole puts it while he smokes Marlboro Lights on the porch, “men and boys are not doing well. And they have not been doing well for a long time.” The evidence supporting this is manifold: Young men are less likely than their female counterparts to finish high school and then enroll in college. They’re dropping out of the job market, and they’re more likely to report loneliness and isolation, as well as more likely to die by suicide.

Part of the problem is the manosphere, the social media ecosystem populated by looksmaxxers, incels, AI-touting hustle bros, and peptide-injecting fitness influencers. Initially a relatively fringe coalition, the “manosphere” has evolved into an online force to be reckoned with, thanks to the massive success of influencers like Jordan Peterson, a former academic who has advocated for all-meat diets and climate-change denialism; and, later, Andrew Tate, a failed kickboxer turned minor webcam impresario, who is currently facing more than 40 criminal charges in the UK and Romania, including trafficking and sex crimes. By preaching traditional masculinity as a path toward self-empowerment, so-called manosphere influencers have appealed to an audience of young men disillusioned by the rise of identity politics. Social media algorithms have happily amplified that message: By 2023, clips featuring Tate had more than 13 billion views on social media platforms.

Left to right: Jonathan Jacobs, Chris Petrone, and Johnny Cole collaborate on a social media house-tour video.

During the 2024 election, an estimated 67 percent of white male zoomers voted for Trump, resulting in a flurry of discourse about the manosphere’s power in channeling the frustrations of young men. “[They’ve] never had brotherhood or friendship,” Cole tells me. “They’ve never had another man look them in the eyes and say they’re worthy.” Men like Tate are successful, he says, because they “weaponize this insecurity and this fragility and give them a scapegoat and say, ‘If you buy my course and you learn how to drop-ship, or come to my alphas-only elite men's circle, then you’ll become a high-value man.’”

Of the three Hey Brother House leaders, Cole is the only one in the demographic the creators are trying to reach. He’s 6'4" and built like a varsity swimmer, with translucent green eyes, gray-painted nails, and light brown hair, which he dyes green and magenta for a short while after he leaves the house. He characterizes his work trying to reach young men as something akin to a divine calling.

“I’m a white man who was a college rugby player, and I do jujitsu, but I also wear earrings and talk about feminism online,” he tells me. “Some of these guys think I’m performative, but in my experience, when I work with men and boys in person, they love me. They've never experienced a man who's a near peer who calls them into accountability, who offers them hugs and encouragement and support. In a looksmaxxing world, for these young guys I’m someone to look up to, literally and figuratively.”

This is where the Hey Brother House comes in: to teach progressive-leaning, male creators how to create content that captures the attention of the Kick-streaming, Zyn-sucking, butt-cut-sporting contingent. The goal is to adopt the visual hallmarks of the manosphere—slick editing, dynamic hooks, fast-paced montages—and apply those to what the house calls “healthy masculinity” content: dudes thrift-shopping together and picking out outfits, or guys playing golf while also wearing pink. “What we're not gonna do is stand in front of a camera, wag our fingers, and say, ‘I think that the patriarchy is the fucking worst thing in the world,’” Cole says.

Of course, there’s plenty of content for young men on social media that does not encourage men to become webcam pimps or forcefully hit themselves in the face with hammers, a la Clavicular. But much of the content in the “healthy masculinity” space is filled with academic jargon and feminist buzzwords. Or it’s more along the lines of Joe Rogan–infused, “Thunderdome-style” masculinity. (Think Instagram posts of white men with tribal tattoos weeping in the desert, with a caption promoting an online crypto investing class.) The Hey Brother House aims to teach male influencers how to promote values like empathy and vulnerability, via content about wrestling or fitness or style or financial advice. “It’s sugar with the medicine,” Cole says.

An activity at the Hey Brother House where members offer gifts to the group and request actions they would like to receive from others.

In selecting the initial cohort for the Hey Brother House, Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs had to strike a delicate balance: They wanted creators who would be “mission-aligned,” as Jacobs put it, but who don’t exclusively make political content. Out of more than 130 applicants, they selected eight men. Some were leftist commentators like Jerry Zeng (133,000 Instagram followers), a 29-year-old, tatted, Jacquemus shorts-wearing video essayist from Houston, and Ian Lightfoot (1 million Instagram followers), an immaculately-eyebrowed, now 26-year-old whose Instagram bio proffers “positivity, popcorn, and bite-sized politics.” Others were more conventional lifestyle influencers like Sean Jones, a premed student who makes cute date-night videos and productivity vlogs, and the Houston-based trainer Stephen Marmolejos (180,000 TikTok followers), who posts fitness content and does sponcon for brands like Corona and Thayers. One, the artist and dancer Mars Wright (195,000 TikTok followers), is a trans man who has never lived in a house with cis men before. “I kind of feel like I’m entering the cafeteria scene in Mean Girls,” he told me before he got to Denver.

I arrive at the house from my hotel to find the guys midway through a vulnerability exercise in the living room. (For four days, I was given almost total access but was politely asked not to attend the first day of exercises, so the men could bond.)

I quietly take a seat on a corduroy couch as the men stand in two parallel lines, facing their partners and taking turns answering the question: “What would you know if you really knew me?” All speaking at once, they say things like: “my father,” “my angry feelings,” “even my best relationship,” “Weight Watchers.” They are mic’d, and the cameras are out in full force, zooming in as the men embrace and thank each other for listening. Some are crying.

Later, the guys sit in a talking circle—one of many I would witness—and unpack their feelings. This is the first time some of them, particularly the brawnier health-and-fitness influencer types, have had such intimate conversations with other men, talking about their marriages, surviving domestic violence, trauma, addiction. “I started out with vague surface-level things that were quirky,” Monteon says afterward, “but at the very end I felt safe enough, and I revealed way more than I expected to.”

Cole, who leads the exercise, nods empathetically. “You can’t heal if you don’t reveal,” he says, the men snapping in assent. (There is a lot of affirmative snapping at the house; there is also repeated use of terms like “aligned,” “affirmed,” and “container,” a reference to a therapeutic trauma-processing modality. I heard about containers a dozen times, only once in the context of a physical vessel.)

The next morning, when I meet the guys for the first full day’s activity—a trip to a thrift store where the men select outfits for each other—approximately 40 percent of them are hungover from karaoke the night before, as well as the day of emotional disclosures. (As Zeng put it to me, “there’s been a lot of trauma-dumping.”) But they seem genuinely psyched for the activity, which is intended to culminate in filming a wholesome “dress your bro for a night out”–type video.

Journaling is a popular practice at the Hey Brother House.

“It’s a lot of pressure. I’ve never shopped for another dude, [or] heard a man compliment another man’s outfit,” Chris Petrone (1.6 million TikTok followers), tells me. “At first I was nervous, but then I was like, let’s get funky.” A baby-faced 31-year-old who lives in Florida, Petrone is one of the most successful creators in the Hey Brother House, thanks in part to a 2021 viral video in which he advocated for men to stock tampons in their bathrooms for female guests; for about a year, he had “the CEO of tampons” in his bio.

If they are nervous, they don’t show it. Monteon, who arrives in a Movember cap and brown sweats, leaves with jeans and a brown and white geometric-patterned button-down, looking like a 1970s Tiger Beat centerfold. And when Lightfoot tries on a purple and yellow cropped windbreaker, Wright and Josh Kennedy, a 29-year-old mustachioed, Wichita-based personal trainer, snap in assent. “That was literally made for you,” Kennedy says.

The Hey Brother House was conceived, at least in part, as a content incubator. But aside from the documentary film crew being present for almost every activity, not a ton of content is actually being made. Occasionally, I turn a corner and see guys editing footage on a laptop or someone filming multiple takes of a house tour in the foyer.

Instead, the dudes seemed focused on … being dudes. They played Mario Kart and went for runs. They talked about what dog breeds they would be. “I am not a scary dog,” Jones said. “And I do believe I am majestic at times.”

Even Wright, who was initially anxious about living in a house with cis men—some of whom had never met a trans man before—quickly bonded with the other members. “I've always wanted to be in community with other men and feel like I belonged and like I was one of them,” he says. “And honestly, I didn’t really believe that a lot of men were having these conversations until I was behind closed doors with them.”

The bros are sitting in the living room for a content brainstorming session. They are watching a slew of manosphere clips, which Cole says embody the three “Rs” of masculinity: “relentlessly rich and ripped.” He then shows a few examples of Reels that he identifies as “really brother-core coded”: a challenge video of men guessing the drinks that have been thrown in their faces, or tips for how men can protect their girlfriends from drink-spiking at bars. The goal, says Jacobs, is not to “attack the messenger” by making fun of Andrew Tate or Jordan Peterson because “that puts people on the defensive.” The men volley around a few ideas, which are similarly wholesome and tongue-in-cheek: golf cart racing, a parody of Jordan Peterson, rating each other’s hugs.

Then Wright pitches an idea for an “ask a trans person” video series, and the warm brotherly vibes start to shift. Wright prefaces his pitch by saying that, during his time in the house, a few of the other members had unintentionally “asked him questions that you should never ask a trans person.” Though he doesn’t name names or call anyone out specifically, he proposes that the snafu serves as a teaching moment for cisgender men watching Hey Brother House content.

“Trans people don’t believe that any cis men care about them at all,” Wright says. “I want to show my community that there are men who care for them and would stand up for them and would be willing to be put in a situation that makes them a little uncomfortable.”

Many of the guys are on board, but Cole visibly bristles at the suggestion, saying the idea causes him “reservation [and] anxiety” due to the possibility of it generating backlash from LGBTQ viewers.

The group holds a meeting to talk through a conflict that has caused tension. Facing camera, left to right: Chris Petrone and Johnny Cole. Facing away, from left to right: Ian Lightfoot and Jerry Zeng.

“I wasn’t worried about being canceled,” he tells me later. “I was worried about the emotional and energetic impact of that series when we, as a container of men, had not addressed the emotional and energetic impact of things that had been said offline.” But this wasn’t how Wright interpreted it. “I was really shocked he reacted like that,” he says. “He’s one of the few cis men to say that trans people really belong, and he invited me here, which was a dream come true. And it’s so gut-wrenchingly painful to see somebody react to you like, ‘Well, I don’t know how this is going to make me look.’”

The impact of the conflict doesn’t become clear until the next day, when members of the House are abruptly summoned upstairs for a “tribunal.”

The vibes are off almost immediately. The House members clearly have no idea what the purpose of the meeting is and are even more flummoxed when one of the camera crew members asks them to head back down and come up again, so they can get a better take. They sit in a circle, baffled, as Echelman, not Cole, opens the meeting by reading a seven-minute statement off his iPhone. Echelman, the documentarian, has largely been absent from the House activities. He occasionally chimes in during meetings and with video pitches during the brainstorm, including “a haunted house, but the ghosts are subverting gender expectations.”

“In line with safety and consent, some things have arisen over the course of the house around conflict that I think it's important to not shy away from, but welcome and embrace and talk through,” he reads. “Rather than let that pass quietly, we want to name how we hold conflict here. Conflict isn't a failure of this space. It's where we practice communication, accountability, and care. And holding space means letting someone name their experience without filtering it.” Then Echelman opens the floor for questions.

On the third floor, the day after the tense emotional group meeting, all that remains is a box of tissues.

Immediately, someone says that they’re confused. “I echo that sentiment,” Cole says. “Are there things that you would like to name that you have observed in this space which prompted you to write that and call this meeting?”

Echelman’s explanation lasts an additional five minutes, over the course of which two things gradually become clear to everyone present: (1) this meeting is about Cole, and (2) he had no idea. Echelman accuses Cole of unintentionally abusing his leadership position to shut people down, and he brings up a critique raised by one house member that the “dress your bro” thrifting activity could be perceived on social media as “poverty porn” or depriving resources from low-income communities. (Echelman’s own “haunted house for toxic masculinity” pitch is not specifically mentioned.) “In a leadership position, it's our responsibility to, even if we’re feeling something in the moment, not to make it about us but someone else being so vulnerable and opening up to us,” he says.

The tribunal, several house members told me afterward, was a disaster. As the men splinter off to go rock-climbing or golfing, Lightfoot tells me, “It felt less like an authentic conversation and more like a reality TV show.” A visibly upset Wright says he had confronted Cole privately about the brainstorm and specifically told Echelman that he did not want to have a meeting in front of the cameras with the group about what happened. To hear him tell it, he was less angry than disappointed. “Their hearts are in the right place,” he says of the House leaders. “They’re working tooth and nail, day and night, to make a difference. But we’re still so far from where we need to be.”

Later, Echelman will dispute others’ characterization of the tribunal: “Plenty of people after the conversation said that we broke the glass ceiling, because we could finally be open and honest with one another,” he tells me later.

He isn’t entirely wrong. After the initial confrontation with Cole, some of the men brought up their own minor conflicts from Hey Brother House. Without exception, they had been addressed graciously and without grandstanding. There was no bluster for the cameras, no aggression, no dick-measuring; none of what you would come to expect from a group of men in conflict with each other. They listened. They affirmed. They told each other how grateful they were for the experience of being there together. Even if the house leaders were in conflict, the creators themselves were “synced up completely,” Wright tells me. “I look at any one of them, and I know they would make me feel safe and comfortable.” It didn’t necessarily make for compelling content, but it did seem like they had taken Cole’s earlier lesson to heart: you can’t heal if you don’t reveal. (Snaps).

Josh Kennedy (left) and Johnny Cole have a heartfelt conversation while doing the dishes.

Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs are now selecting the cohort for the next House, which will take place in Austin in December, followed by a third in Atlanta. Nearly all eight are already confirmed, including leftist bodybuilder Colin Davis and trans former NCAA athlete Schuyler Bailar. The leaders have apparently hashed things out and are working to correct some of the mistakes they made with the Denver House, enlisting the services of an in-person, trained men’s group facilitator to mediate conflicts. “This is a test-and-learn pilot,” Jacobs tells me. “While we are comfortable with swings and misses, we also want to ensure we don’t keep taking the same swing.” Cole’s friend, whom he describes as a “professional race car driver and videographer,” will also be on hand to record social media content. “He's 22 and has a really vibey aesthetic,” he says. “He knows what's t-u-f-f, tuff.”

All told, the creators at the Hey Brother House produced somewhere between 65 and 70 videos. The main focus was on bonding activities and group discussions. The highest-performing video was a clip of Wright injecting himself with testosterone as the other men cheered him on, which got 689,000 views. After the tribunal, the House also produced his “Ask a Trans Man” video series, which overperformed on both Instagram and Wright’s YouTube channel; in one, Cole and Wright, who have since made up, were prominently featured.

Little of the content from Hey Brother House went viral, but for a handful of the creators, their audience now skews more male; Wright, for instance, says some of his content from the house reached a predominantly male audience. But in reaching their target demo—men from 18 to 25—they saw little success. “There are some ways in which our content was too on the nose,” says Cole. In the future, he says they’ll make more of “the type of stuff that young men want to see” — such as the wrestling videos, which he says overperformed. For this reason, they’re trying to recruit a much younger cohort for Austin, who focus less on political commentary and more on skits and lifestyle content. They’re having some difficulty: many younger male creators often have to juggle their content creation with school. A lot of them have talent managers who don’t want their clients to “get too political,” or have turned down the House because they can’t pay them that much.

Josh Kennedy (left) cheers on Johnny Cole and Ian Lightfoot as they hug after their dance-off performances at The Movement Project.

But there are signs pointing in the direction of a healthier version of manhood being promoted on social media—or, at the very least, an exhaustion with older models. Following the midterm elections in November, men like senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, and Sen. Jon Ossoff emerged triumphant at the polls, proffering a kindler and gentler (not to mention hunkier) model of masculinity than any proffered by a Clavicular or an Androgenic. Perhaps even more tellingly, white men between the ages of 18 and 29, who had previously helped deliver the 2024 election to Trump, swung overwhelmingly left. According to one analysis, 54 percent of this bracket voted for Democratic House candidates.

There was also one video that came out of Denver that did indeed perform well with the target demographic of Gen Z men. A simple, five-second looping Instagram Reel shows Kennedy and Cole locked in an embrace. “When’s the last time you got a hug longer than 5 seconds?” the onscreen text reads. It has garnered 500,000 views, mostly from 18-to-24-year-olds.

I am reminded of something Cole told me the first time we spoke about how to solve the toxic masculinity crisis. “I know so strongly in my soul that more men and boys just need more hugs,” he said. “No matter what you’ve been through, no matter who you are. You just need more hugs [and] safe touches and affirmation and encouragement.” At the time, this struck me as cringe, and maybe a bit too simplistic. Watching the Reel with Kennedy and Cole embracing, I feel the same. But that doesn’t mean it’s not also true.

#370. Target shares rise 7% as retailer posts best sales growth in five years, hikes guidance

Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.

The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.

"[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.

Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.

Encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.

The company also said it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90.

"The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time."

Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier.

This year, the company said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year.

On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.

The company said it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season.

Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround.

As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.

The big-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.

It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer said on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter.

Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

#368. FIFA presidential election 2027: Infantino facing Diallo and Tashima — could an alliance change everything?

Two challengers to Gianni Infantino have registered for next year's FIFA presidential election. What do Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima stand for – and do they stand a chance against the incumbent?

Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 member nations of FIFA, soccer's global governing body, cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027. DW looks at the field of candidates.

Gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era. Under Infantino's leadership, FIFA's revenues have continued to grow, the Club World Cup has been revamped, and the men's World Cup has been expanded to include 48 teams.

During his decade in office, the 56-year-old Swiss has built a global network of support. Infantino enjoys significant backing in Africa, South America, and large parts of Asia — a result of multi-billion-dollar development programs and financial grants provided to national associations. Many smaller member associations view him as a president who takes their interests more seriously than his predecessors did.

At the same time, critics accuse Infantino of consolidating power within the organization around himself. During his tenure, oversight and control bodies have been restructured multiple times, and key positions have been filled with his own loyalists.

Infantino's ostentatious closeness to political leaders has also sparked debate — whether exemplified by his conduct during the World Cup in Qatar, his tight ties to Saudi Arabia or his public appearances alongside US President Donald Trump (though that relationship is said to have cooled significantly after the 2026 World Cup). Detractors accuse him of seeking proximity to authoritarian rulers and intermingling political interests too closely with football.

A failed initiative to grant private investors a larger stake in lucrative FIFA competitions (FIFA Forward Enterprise) has also placed Infantino under considerable pressure. As the FIFA election approaches, he faces the prospect of legal challenges; European football's governing body UEFA is aiming to take action over the investment plan, while other critics are calling for an investigation by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

However, his time in office has brought many of FIFA's 211 member associations additional development funding and other revenue. This makes him the man to beat in the March vote.

Philippe Diallo is Europe's candidate. The 63-year-old, who was elected president of the French Football Federation in 2023, is seen as an experienced sports administrator with a pragmatic and measured leadership style.

He has the backing of UEFA, as well as many of its 55 member associations, including the German Football Association (DEB).

"Philippe Diallo stands for a version of football that embraces responsibility and tackles future challenges with determination," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said in a statement announcing the German FA's position.

"We want a FIFA that serves the sport in the interest of all its member associations. That is why we support Philippe Diallo with great conviction."

Diallo is positioning himself as a clear alternative to Infantino. His supporters see him as a candidate who stands for sound leadership, transparency, and a stronger dialogue with member associations. Unlike the incumbent, however, he lacks a global network of allies.

The third man in the race is Kozo Tashima. The 68-year-old was president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024 and has been one of the most influential officials in Asia for decades.

During a press conference in the Japanese capital Tokyo on Friday, Tashima mentioned the words "integrity, fairness, trust and transparency" several times in explaining his decision to run.

"I just don't only want to be the FIFA president, my intention is to make FIFA better," he said.

"Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organization."

Tashima also acknowledged that failing to have won the endorsement of any of the regional confederations — the Asian Football Confederation is supporting Infantino — makes him a longshot to win the election.

But he could still play a key role in the outcome. At a press conference on Tuesday, Diallo said he intended to reach out to Tashima to "unite forces" to defeat Infantino. Tashima hasn't ruled out the notion.

"We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he's a great person to team up with," he said.

"Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management," he added.

However, Tashima also noted that he hadn't had any thoughts of withdrawing from the race.

If Infantino's challengers do manage to join forces in some way, they might just stand a chance of upsetting the highly favored incumbent.

#364. Best Laptops for Travel (2026): Which to Take on the Road

As a laptop reviewer, I have plenty of devices to choose from when I travel for work. In some cases, my favorite overall laptop doesn’t translate into the one I want to travel with. When I’m squeezed into a plane, I’ll choose maximum battery life and portability over features like a bigger screen or more ports.

Fortunately, there are many great travel laptops, and you’ll still appreciate them when you aren’t on the road. Of the hundreds of laptops I’ve tested in my life, here are the ones I always choose to travel with.

If there’s an obvious pick for the best travel laptop, it’s the Dell XPS 13. It’s been the best compact laptop you can buy for years, and that’s even more true in its latest incarnation. The key dimension to pay attention to on the XPS 13 is the depth, which is crucial for air travel. At 7.9 inches, it’s among the smallest laptops you can buy. Those economy-class seat-back tray tables on airplanes are only around 10 inches deep, and while that’s technically enough to accommodate even a 16-inch MacBook Pro, whether you can actually open the lid and use the laptop is another question. The XPS 13 is even smaller than the MacBook Neo, despite having a larger screen.

The XPS 13 achieves this by using a 13.4-inch display (measured diagonally), compared to many of the 14-inch laptops on this list. Second, it has very narrow bezels around that screen, minimizing the device’s overall footprint. While 14-inch laptops have become more popular in recent years, that bigger display size also increases the overall footprint—and every millimeter counts when working on a plane. The XPS 13 still has enough room for your palms when typing (unless you have huge hands), and the keyboard is among my favorites to type on.

The other two major advantages for travel are weight and battery life. This little laptop only weighs 2.2 pounds, a full half-pound lighter than the 13-inch MacBook Air. You might forget you have it in your backpack while traveling.

Now, the XPS 13 isn't the most powerful laptop in the world—at least not the cheaper models. The standard version comes with only 8 GB of RAM and an Intel chip with only two Performance cores. It’s good enough for basic web tasks, but for real work, you might run into limitations. You can address this by opting for the 16 GB model (which keeps the price under $1,000) or upgrading to the much more powerful Core Ultra 7 355 processor. The latter is much more expensive and comes with twice the storage, but it doesn’t add extra weight or size. Regardless of the chip you choose, the XPS 13 gets absolutely fantastic battery life. It depends on what you're doing with it, but you could easily work through a long international flight without worrying about plugging in.

If weight is your primary concern, the Asus Zenbook A14 is another contender. Despite being larger overall than the XPS 13 (with a bigger screen), the Zenbook A14 weighs 2.16 pounds—a hair lighter than the Dell. That’s seriously impressive, and I still remember how astounded I was when I first picked it up. Asus debuts its “ceraluminum” material in the chassis, which gives you the sturdiness of aluminum with the lightness of plastic. It’s not quite as rigid as metal, but it’s not as flimsy as ultra-light laptops in the past.

If you’re less worried about working on the plane and more about lugging a laptop around, the Zenbook A14 is a good choice. The Zenbook A14 has several advantages over the XPS 13 that can be helpful on the go, including built-in ports like a headphone jack, USB-A, and HDMI. If you’re working out of a remote office or presenting to a client, these can definitely come in handy. The XPS 13 only has two USB-C ports and nothing else.

There are a number of different versions of the Asus Zenbook A14 floating around out there. I’d stay away from the 8 GB model Asus sells and opt for the 16 GB model instead. There’s also a newer model that uses the Snapdragon X2 Elite chip, but I don’t think it’s worth the extra $450—especially not for a laptop focused on travel.

The 13-inch MacBook Air also makes a great travel laptop. It’s relatively small, thanks to its 13.6-inch screen.

In terms of portability, its main advantage over the XPS 13 and Zenbook A14 is its thinness. At 0.42 inches, it’s the thinnest laptop out there—and it doesn’t stick huge rubber feet on the bottom to compensate like other laptops do, such as the Razer Blade 14. You might not think thickness matters much in a travel laptop, but if you’re squeezing stuff into a backpack, every extra millimeter matters.

The MacBook Neo is also worth mentioning here. It’s not quite as thin as the MacBook Air, but because its screen is 0.4 inches smaller, it has a more compact overall footprint. Battery life is the bigger issue when taking the Neo on a trip, as it doesn’t last as long as the MacBook Air or Dell XPS 13. The 8 GB of RAM limitation doesn’t affect its use as a travel laptop much, but it's something to consider for a work laptop in general. That said, it has a very pretty screen for a laptop at this price.

Budget laptops aren’t typically known for being particularly lightweight and travel-worthy. Most of them struggle, especially with battery life. The HP OmniBook 5 might be an exception. You can usually find it on sale for under $700, even with 16 GB of RAM and an OLED display.

The OmniBook 5 isn’t quite as compact as the MacBook Neo because of its larger screen, but it is also half an inch thick and weighs only 2.8 pounds. The Snapdragon X Plus also delivers solid battery life, plenty to feel comfortable traveling with. It’s not a laptop without compromises (like the poor touchpad), but it comes with 16 GB of RAM, unlike some other laptops at this price. That’s a solid deal if you need something to travel with on a budget.

Good question. Tablets can make for great travel devices because of their size and ease of use. If you need a proper keyboard and touchpad—and the app support to handle a typical workday—you’re probably better off getting a laptop.

The Surface Pro 12 is the two-in-one laptop I’d recommend first. It’s absolutely tiny for a computer, even though it runs the full version of Windows 11. Even with the detachable keyboard connected, it weighs only 1.8 pounds. The only real problem with bringing this on a plane is the kickstand, which adds some extra depth. It’s just small enough that it should fit while open on an airplane tray table, unlike the 13.8-inch Surface Pro model.

Of course, that kickstand is also a huge advantage for the Surface Pro 12 if you’re using it without the keyboard. While that would make work difficult, it’s ideal for watching movies. Set this up on your tray table with some movies downloaded, and you’ll be the envy of your aisle. And when you need to get some work done in a coffee shop or at a smaller table, you’ll be happy to have access to the keyboard and touchpad—both of which are very comfortable to use. Just know that it's sold separately.

The iPad Air, paired with the Magic Keyboard, avoids the Surface Pro 12’s kickstand issue. And with only an 11-inch screen, it’s perfect for use in small spaces—with or without the keyboard (note that there is also a 13-inch version). If you can accomplish all your work on an iPad, more power to ya! The iPad Air should give you everything you need, so long as you get the Magic Keyboard. If your travels involve more leisurely activities, the iPad Air is a great device for reading by the pool or for playing games.

One benefit of this latest version of the iPad Air is not only its performance (thanks to the M4 chip inside) but also the front-facing camera, which has been moved to landscape for more natural-feeling video calls. Of course, you could also opt for the 11-inch iPad Pro for extra performance (and the incredible tandem OLED screen). It’s also slightly thinner and lighter, though I don't think it's worth the significant price difference.

Lastly, there’s definitely room here for laptops with 360-degree hinges—a different class of two-in-one laptops. I haven’t tested a recent Windows device with this form factor that I truly loved, but there’s no question it works well on an airplane. Just fold the screen back with the keyboard face down, and you have the perfect screen for watching movies. The Lenovo Yoga 9i 14 is a gorgeous option, though it’s incredibly expensive right now. But if you can afford it, you’ll love the 2-in-1 action combined with one of the slickest designs imaginable. The Framework Laptop 12 is also worth considering. While it’s a bit thick and heavy for a travel laptop, its smaller screen, touchscreen, and 360-degree hinge make it a good option. It’s also one of the cheaper options available, and it’s user-upgradeable.

Whether you’re packing for a trip across the world or across the state, a proper travel laptop shouldn’t be heavy or overly large. That rules out 15-inch and 16-inch laptops, which are so big you can’t use them on airplane tray tables or at coffee shops. But even when you narrow it down to 14-inch laptops or smaller, there are three portability factors to consider.

When you’re on the go, you want a laptop that doesn’t constantly make you worry about finding an outlet. Bringing a laptop power bank can help, but the biggest factor in staying sane while traveling is a device that can stay on. Many factors affect how long a laptop can last, including CPU efficiency, battery wattage, screen brightness and resolution, and more.

Long-lasting laptops, such as the Dell XPS 13, will get you through a long flight. The processor is the main thing to look out for. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X series of chips are battery-efficient, as are Apple’s M-series chips. Intel also has some highly efficient CPUs in its most recent lineup, though you’ll need to pay close attention to the model number, as it can vary wildly depending on the specific CPU you’re using. To dig deeper, read my extensive guide on How to Buy the Right Laptop, which breaks down different CPU options.

The size of seat-back tray tables varies. There’s no exact size because of various factors, such as the airline, aircraft, cabin, and seat. Remember: Just because a laptop can physically fit on a tray table doesn’t mean you’ll have space to open and use it. With that in mind, here are the general averages to keep in mind. Airlines do not list tray table sizes, but you can expect one in economy to measure around 16 x 9 inches, while premium cabins will have larger tables depending on the seat.

I’ve included both tablets and laptops in my recommendations, but your choice will depend on why you’re traveling with a device. If it’s for a vacation and you really only need a device to read, watch, and play on (perhaps with the occasional email check), a tablet works perfectly. Lounging with a tablet, whether on a plane or by the pool, feels much more leisurely than using a laptop. More importantly, it'll help you avoid dipping back into work mode. Whether an Android tablet, iPad, or Windows tablet, just pair it with a compatible keyboard case—and you’re good to go.

However, if you’re traveling for work (or need to work while traveling), a proper laptop will be better. The one you already have may work just fine, but frequent fliers know they prefer a more compact device. And more specifically, a small laptop with a keyboard and trackpad will work better on your lap or on small desks than a tablet.

#363. Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV

In the latest in a series of raids and arrests, another major pro-opposition Turkish broadcaster has been brought under state control. This is the third in a year.

Another important opposition media outlet in Turkey has been placed under state control. On Tuesday morning, authorities raided the offices of the television broadcaster Sozcu TV and the news portal Sozcu.com.tr, and arrested several executives.

A trustee has also been appointed: The state deposit protection fund, TMSF, which usually administers the assets of insolvent companies, has been put in charge. Sozcu was one of the last big media companies in Turkey to regularly report critically on the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

A large police contingent raided the broadcaster's headquarters in Istanbul, with counterterrorism officers searching the offices. According to Sozcu, its chairwoman, Funda Tuncer Sidali, and Asim Akgul, the former chief executive of the Sozcu group, were among those arrested.

The broadcaster did not initially announce the appointment of the trustee on its digital channels. It did call on its audience to follow it under a new account. The leader of the main opposition party, Ozgur Ozel, declared on X: "You will never be able to prevent this nation's voice from rising, its rebellion from being heard, its cry from echoing."

The Istanbul public prosecutor's office has confirmed the arrangements. It justified the investigation with claims of a suspected connection between the owner of Sozcu, Burak Akhay, and the Gülen movement. The Turkish government blames this movement, which was once allied to Erdogan, for the attempted coup in 2016, and has designated it a terrorist organization.

According to the investigators, Akbay is said to have used foreign bank accounts to finance two companies involved in media activities on behalf of the Gülen movement. They claim there is strong suspicion that he was able, in this way, to hold a leadership position in the organization.

It is not new for the Turkish state to take over media organizations by appointing trustees. Many media companies accused of being close to the Gülen movement were brought under state control in this way after the attempted coup in 2016. What is new is that for about a year now this is also happening to media seen as pro-opposition.

Sozcu is not the first opposition broadcaster to be targeted by the authorities. The TELEI TV channel was searched on October 24, 2025. Its editor-in-chief, Merdan Yanardag, was arrested on charges of espionage and remains in custody. The offices of Halk TV were raided on October 14 this year. There, too, a trustee was put in charge.

In the space of just over a year, three of the most important opposition television channels have been brought under state control. Observers see this as another step toward an increasingly authoritarian and politically isolated system.

Berk Esen, a political scientist with Sabanci University in Istanbul, sees these measures as a significant weakening of the opposition in the public domain.

Esen told DW that the government may first have acted behind the scenes and tried to bring Sozcu to heel politically. When this didn't succeed, it invoked the judiciary. Esen says Turkey is increasingly moving toward an authoritarian system. The attempt to prevent opposition organizations and media from gaining strength and influence is part of this.

Esen describes the opposition's success in local government elections in March 2024 as a political turning point. Since then, he says, the government has seen its chances of winning political competitions at the ballot box receding. "It's become harder for the AKP to win elections," says Esen. "That's why it's attacking the opposition and the free media both at once."

Several opposition mayors have also been arrested in recent months and replaced by trustees. They include the mayor of Istanbul and presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu, who has been in detention since his arrest in March last year. He is regarded as one of Erdogan's most promising challengers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Turkish Journalists' Association (TGC) spoke of a "black winter for press freedom," and announced its solidarity with all those affected. It described the recent developments as a serious attack on press freedom. The fact that a trustee had been appointed, first at Halk TV and now at Sozcu, showed how the media climate in Turkey has deteriorated, it said.

"These days, too, shall pass," the TGC declared. "When that day comes, those journalists who seek the truth today will be remembered, as will the decisions that prevent the public from hearing that truth."

This article has been translated from German.

#361. Shania Twain calls for equal pay and more diversity in country music

Shania Twain is standing up for others in country music.

The legendary star in the genre used her acceptance speech for the Equal Play Award at Sunday’s CMT Awards to call for more equity and diversity in the country music industry.

“When I wrote the phrase ‘Man I feel like a woman’ I honestly had no idea at the time it would become an undercurrent of a decades-long career,” she said, referring to one of her biggest hits. “It’s amazing how one statement can empower so many.”

The phrase, Twain said, “has been adopted by an array of fantastic communities all around the world and become a genuine path of power…which brings me so much joy.”

“I believe in an all-inclusive country music. We’re family,” Twain said. “This is a genre of music with a rich history that raised and nurtured my own songwriting and performance and recording career from childhood. Currently, the industry standard does a real disservice to this.”

Twain, who was presented the award by rapper Megan Thee Stallion, shouted out some of the diverse acts she is spotlighting on her “Queen of Me” tour this year, including Lily Rose, Lindsay Ell, Hailey Whitters, Mickey Guyton and others.

“I will continue to do my best as a trailblazer,” Twain said. “Together, let’s ensure all our fellow artists get equal play regardless of gender, age or race.”

She also performed acappella with the African American singing group, The BoykinZ, while presenting an award onstage. Twain connected with the group, who are sisters and rising country stars, after Kelly Clarkson surprised them recently by bringing Twain out to meet them during an episode of Clarkson’s daytime talk show.

#360. Hims & Hers launches new peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it announced the new products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

The new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October launched an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a company spokesperson said in a statement.

None of the company's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims said they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy."

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

The company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

Hims said it plans to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The company also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized plan to their needs, if appropriate.

The company said it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

"If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options."

However, Vinjamoori said there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

"We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he said. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a company of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead."

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He said Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight."

But health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," said Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body."

Kritzer said the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, said Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide users, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler said one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?"

But he said the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

That appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The company says patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

Hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that says the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

In practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "big fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

There is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

Meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data shows only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione showed that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also said in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

All of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.
